title: Fossils Show an Early Human Relative Lived in Africa Earlier Than Thought
summary:
New fossils from a cave in South Africa are adding to the story of early human evolution. Scientists say they give stronger evidence that Homo erectus, an early human relative, lived in southern Africa about 2 million years ago. That is roughly 200,000 years earlier than many researchers had long believed.

Homo erectus is the first species that most scientists agree belongs to our own group, called Homo. It is likely one of our direct ancestors.

The fossils come from Drimolen, a cave site in an area known as the Cradle of Humankind, one of the richest places in the world for ancient human fossils. The site was dug from 1992 to 2019, but many fossils found there had never been fully described. A team led by researchers at La Trobe University in Australia, working with scientists in South Africa and the United States, has now studied 18 more of them.

One of the fossils is part of an adult Homo erectus skull. An earlier Homo erectus fossil from Drimolen belonged to a young child, so scientists were not sure what adults looked like. Lead researcher Jesse Martin said the new fossil helps confirm the species first appeared there 2 million years ago.

The cave also holds fossils of another relative, Paranthropus robustus. It had a smaller brain, but over about 200,000 years it grew even bigger back teeth and stronger chewing muscles for crushing tough food. Meanwhile, Homo erectus was developing a larger brain and smaller teeth.

Martin said that at Drimolen, Paranthropus robustus outnumbered Homo erectus by more than 10 to one. Back then, he said, our ancestors looked like the "long-odds chance to survive." The study appears in the journal Annals of Human Biology.
why_it_matters: Each new fossil helps fill gaps in the story of how humans evolved, and this one suggests our ancestors' history in Africa began earlier than many scientists thought.

background_read: Fossils are the preserved remains of living things from long ago, and scientists use them to learn how life has changed over time.
Humans belong to a group called Homo, and several related species lived in Africa long before modern humans appeared.
South Africa's Cradle of Humankind is a region of caves where many important fossils of human relatives have been found.
Scientists date fossils by studying the rocks and layers around them, which helps them tell when a species first appeared.
